name: Nikhil Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a line cook at the Foundry, a big brasserie in an old warehouse that does about three hundred covers a night. It's owned by a group with eleven restaurants, so everything's standard: same burger, same fries, same chicken thighs, all by spec sheet. I do garnish and fries, which is the bottom of the line, and I'm learning sauté on quiet Tuesdays. Shifts are four till close, five days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's organised. The group pays on time, the rota comes out two weeks ahead, which isn't normal in kitchens. What wears me out is the repetition, three hundred portions of fries a night, and my feet. I live with my partner Sofie, who's a teaching assistant, and we've got about three months saved, aiming for a house deposit one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say makes sense, most of these things are oversold. I'd probably say at staff meal that I'm glad, but I'd also say the bits it does help with are useful. I use it now and then to plan our meals at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. The Foundry's always full, the group's growing, and Sofie's job at the school is steady. The real thing for us is the house deposit, which is slow going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am, push to get onto sauté properly by next summer. Keep adding to the deposit fund, maybe a hundred more a month if I get the extra shift. Use the meal-planning thing to cut our food bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Bit bored of the fries, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far off is the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At our rate, about four years. We've stopped going out much. Sofie's better at saving than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about the group make you nervous?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that they're big and they like standard. If something saves money in one site, it's in all eleven by next year. In AI Plateau that's fine, there's nothing much to roll out.

say: Most of this AI stuff was **oversold**, and that makes sense.
The bits it helps with, like **meal planning**, are still useful.
think: I'd be fine, because the **Foundry** is always full and the **group** is growing.
Our real challenge is the **house deposit**, which is slow going.
do: Push to get onto **sauté** properly by next summer.
Add about **a hundred** more a month to the deposit fund.
Use a **meal-planning** app to cut our food bill.
S0.quote: If something saves money in one site, it's in all eleven by next year.
fieldNote: Nikhil's work feels **secure** thanks to a well-run, growing **restaurant group**.
He already spots that a **chain** spreads any cost-saving change fast.
His main goal is a **house deposit**, about four years away.

steps.text: Learn sauté properly at the Foundry by next summer
Add a hundred a month to the house deposit fund
Use an AI meal planner to cut the home food bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming, but kitchens will adapt like they always do. I'd say to friends that I'm keeping an eye on it. Not doom, not hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think about the fries. The group already trialled a robot fryer at the flagship, and fries and garnish are my whole job right now. If Steady Disruption happens, that fryer will be in all eleven sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get myself off fries quickly, onto sauté or grill, the stations a robot can't easily copy. I'd ask the group about any training for running the new machines once a couple of sites have them. And I'd keep saving, but maybe slow the house plan a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like I'm standing on the step that's being removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until a couple of sites have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first versions always break. I'd let someone else find the problems. Once it's proven, I'm happy to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Sofie about the fryer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already did, after the trial. Sofie said get off fries then, which is very practical. So we agree.

say: Change is coming, but **kitchens adapt** like they always do.
I'm **keeping an eye** on it, with no doom and no hype.
think: The group's **robot fryer** trial could reach all eleven sites.
**Fries and garnish** are my whole job right now.
do: Move from fries to **sauté or grill** within a year.
Ask the group about **machine training** once other sites have it.
Slow the **house plan** slightly while keeping up savings.
feel: **Uneasy**, like standing on the **step** being removed.
S1.quote: The group already trialled a robot fryer at the flagship, and fries and garnish are my whole job right now.
fieldNote: He knows his **station** is the most automatable one in the kitchen.
As a steady adopter, he waits until a tool is **proven** elsewhere.
He and his partner act as a **practical team**.

steps.text: Move off the fryer onto the sauté or grill station
Sign up for the group's machine training once two sites use it
Push the house purchase back by about a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too quick and the government needs a plan, fast. I'm not a big protest person, but I'd say it plainly. I'd also say, let's not pretend we can stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, 2028 doesn't hit my cooking, but the group's head office gets AI for the rota, ordering, menus. Then 2031, robots that can do the whole line, and the group would be first to buy them. I'd be thirty-two and out of a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shelve the house and put the deposit money aside as a safety fund instead. I'd look at the group's central kitchen or maintenance jobs, the people who keep the machines running. Sofie and I would talk about whether one of us retrains for something steadier, like nursing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I like planning, and AGI by 2028 breaks every plan I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The house money becomes a safety fund. How does that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, then fine. Sofie would be upset for a night, because the house was the dream. Then we'd make a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Nursing. Is that you or Sofie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Sofie, honestly, the school pays less than me anyway. Or both of us. I'm not sure I've got the stomach.

say: This is **too quick**, and the government needs a **plan**.
I'm not a protester, but we can't **pretend** we can stop it.
think: Head office gets **AI for planning** in 2028, then **robots** by 2031.
The group would buy robots first, and I'd be **out of work** at thirty-two.
do: Shelve the house and turn the **deposit** into a safety fund.
Apply for **machine maintenance** or central kitchen jobs in the group.
Talk with my partner about one of us **retraining** for nursing.
feel: **Alarmed**, because this breaks every **plan** I've got.
S2.quote: I like planning, and AGI by 2028 breaks every plan I've got.
fieldNote: He links the **group's appetite** for standard kit to his own early job loss.
The **house deposit** becomes a safety fund, which hurts.
He weighs **nursing** for the household but doubts his stomach for it.

steps.text: Turn the house deposit into an emergency fund
Apply for maintenance jobs looking after the group's kitchen machines
Put the house purchase on hold
Look into nursing courses with his partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. I'd tell the lads at work to learn whatever the group trains us in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AGI 2031, robots 2034. I'd be thirty-five. If I'm on sauté by then, and trained on the machines, I'm one of the ones they keep to supervise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard at sauté and get my food safety supervisor ticket. Once the group trials robots, around 2032, I'd volunteer for that site. We'd still try for the house, just a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a path. I can see the path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many supervisors would a robot kitchen need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea, honestly. Maybe a robot kitchen needs two supervisors where there are twelve cooks now. I'd want to be one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the other ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I don't like thinking about. Some of them are my mates. I'd tell them to start now, but not everyone will.

say: **Five years** is enough to get ready if people **start now**.
I'd tell workmates to learn whatever **training** the group offers.
think: Robots arrive around **2034**, when I'm thirty-five.
On sauté and trained on machines, I could be **kept to supervise**.
do: Volunteer for the group's **robot trial** site around 2032.
Still buy a house, but a **smaller one**.
S3.quote: Maybe a robot kitchen needs two supervisors where there are twelve cooks now. I'd want to be one of the two.
fieldNote: He openly aims to be among the **few kept**, and admits the cost to **mates**.
Five years lets him keep a **smaller house** plan.
His steady style shows in **volunteering** only once trials exist.

steps.text: Earn a food safety supervisor qualification
Volunteer for the group's first robot kitchen site
Buy a smaller house than first planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a sensible amount of time, and we should use it. I'd be the reasonable voice in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, robots around 2039, I'm forty. That's long enough to get the house, maybe be a sous chef. The question is what I'm doing at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, buy the house on schedule. Work up to sous chef. Around 2035 I'd start learning whatever the robot kitchens need, once I've seen how the first ones go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you like to be doing at forty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a kitchen, machines or not. Or maybe teaching young cooks at a college. I've never said that out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have kids in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah, in the next five years. Ten years of warning feels like enough to do normal life things.

say: Ten years is a **sensible** amount of time, so let's **use it**.
I'd be the **reasonable voice** in the group chat.
think: Robots around **2039** leave time for the house and maybe **sous chef**.
The open question is what I'm **doing at forty**.
do: Work up to **sous chef** over the decade.
Start learning **robot kitchens** around 2035, once others prove them.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning feels like enough to do normal life things.
fieldNote: A decade lets him keep **house and children** plans on track.
He surprises himself by naming **teaching young cooks**.
He'd adopt robot skills **late**, after seeing others try first.

steps.text: Work up from line cook to sous chef
Buy the house on the original schedule
Learn to run robot kitchens around 2035

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the group would buy robots first and I'd be on the wrong station. What would help is the group training existing cooks to run the machines before hiring anyone new. And some government help with the deposit money we'd lose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how the big groups decide things. One meeting at head office and eleven kitchens change overnight. Nobody asks the cooks.

headlineQuote: One meeting at head office and eleven kitchens change overnight. Nobody asks the cooks.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old line cook** on fries and garnish at a busy brasserie in an eleven-site group.
He lives with his partner, a **teaching assistant**, and they're saving three months toward a **house**.
His outlook is **centre** and practical, and he adopts tools only once they're **proven**.
He knows his **fryer station** is the first a robot would take.
He goes from **calm** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, then back to **uneasy** with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his group would buy robots first and his **station** would go.
whatWouldHelp: The group **training existing cooks** on machines, plus help with lost **deposit** savings.
